claims.statement: The black pawns on c6 and c7 are doubled.

hints: Look at the files, not the ranks.
Two pawns of one colour stand on the same file.
It is the c-file.
items.explain: Black's c-pawns stand on c6 and c7, two pawns on one file. That is the price Black pays for the open lines and the bishop pair.

items.prompt: Which side owns the bishop pair here?

claims.statement: Only Black owns a light-squared and a dark-squared bishop.

hints: Count the bishops each side still has.
White gave up a bishop earlier in the line.
Black still has both.
items.explain: White exchanged a bishop for a knight earlier in the line, so only Black keeps two bishops.

items.prompt: White to move. Black left the usual path with a rare knight move. Find the best reply.

claims.statement: At depth 16 the engine's best move is the queen move to e2.
Trading queens on d8 is rated at least 30 centipawns lower.

hints: Black's king has not castled and cannot do so quickly.
Count what each queen move attacks.
The queen goes to the e-file.
items.explain: At depth 16 the queen move to e2 scores about 0.37 above the queen trade; one engine at one depth, so a hint about the plan, not a law.

feedback_by_move.d1d8: The familiar trade, but the engine rates it at least 30 centipawns lower at depth 16 in this position.

items.prompt: White to move in this Closed Ruy Lopez. Choose a move and write the plan it starts.

claims.statement: At depth 16 the engine's best move is one of h3, a4, d4, d3, and all four are within 40 centipawns of it.
The pawn lunge g4 is rated at least 100 centipawns lower.

hints: Several sensible moves are about equal: look for one with a purpose.
Ask what each move prepares, not only what it is.
Ask which side of the board and which piece each move prepares for.
items.explain: Four plans are within 40 centipawns at depth 16, so the score alone cannot choose. The choice is a human one: which plan do you understand best?

feedback_by_move.g2g4: A loosening lunge near your own king; the engine rates it at least 100 centipawns lower at depth 16.

items.prompt: Black to move. White has a bishop and a pawn against a lone king. Can White win by force?

claims.statement: The tablebase says the position is a draw with Black to move.

hints: Count material, then ask where the pawn will promote.
The pawn promotes on h8. Which colour is that square?
The bishop does not control the promotion square.
items.explain: A wrong-coloured bishop plus a rook pawn cannot force the win: the lone king reaches the corner. The tablebase confirms a draw.

items.prompt: Black to move. The same position, but the bishop stands on a dark square. Can White win by force?

claims.statement: The tablebase says Black, to move, loses.

hints: Compare with the first position: what moved?
Which colour is the promotion square h8?
This bishop covers h8.
items.explain: With the bishop on the colour of the promotion square, the corner is no refuge and White wins; the tablebase confirms it.

items.prompt: Black to move. The bishop is still on the wrong colour, but the white king stands on f5 instead of f6, one rank further back. Can White win by force?

claims.statement: The tablebase says the position is a draw with Black to move.

hints: Which feature decided the first position?
Is it the king's square or the bishop's colour?
The bishop is still the wrong colour.
items.explain: The king's square is irrelevant here: with the wrong-coloured bishop the draw remains.

items.prompt: White to move. A machine finds this in a blink. Find the mate in two.

claims.statement: The queen move to b8 leads to a forced mate in two.

hints: Look at the d-file and the black king.
A queen sacrifice removes the only defender.
Queen to b8 with check.
items.explain: The queen gives check, the knight must capture it, and the rook on d1 then mates on d8. The engine confirms the mate in two.

items.prompt: White to move in a closed King's Indian. Four moves, all within 40 centipawns. Choose one and say what plan it prepares.

claims.statement: At depth 16 the engine's best move is one of Ne1, Rb1, a3, Be3, all within 40 centipawns.

hints: Several moves are equal: what does each one prepare?
Which of the four prepares a queenside advance, and which meets Black's kingside pawn push first?
Prepare b4, or prepare to answer f5.
items.explain: Four moves are within 40 centipawns, so the engine cannot name one plan. Rb1 and a3 prepare the b4 push on the queenside; Be3 and Ne1 meet Black's f-pawn break first, so they do not yet pick a wing [I]. Your reasons decide.

items.prompt: Black to move; the knight on d6 is attacked. Which retreat stays in the prepared line?

claims.statement: At depth 16 the knight retreat to f5 is the engine's best move.
The other knight retreat, to e4, is rated at least 30 centipawns lower at depth 16.

hints: The knight must keep an eye on d4 and e3.
Which square is on the edge of the white pawn's reach?
It goes to f5.
items.explain: Black's knight steps to f5; 1,258 of 1,269 top-level games chose it [V]. The other retreat, to e4, was played only 11 times, and the engine rates it worse by roughly half a pawn at depth 16.

feedback_by_move.d6e4: The rare move: memory has nothing to say here and the engine rates it at least 30 centipawns lower at depth 16.

items.prompt: White has just played h3. Tap the square from which Black's c8 bishop could have pinned the knight on f3, and which the h-pawn now covers.

claims.statement: The white pawn on h3 attacks g4.

hints: The bishop on c8 travels on the light-squared diagonal.
The pin needs the bishop in front of the knight.
It is a square on the g-file.
items.explain: A bishop on g4 would pin the knight on f3 to the queen on d1. The pawn on h3 covers g4, so a later d4 will not meet a pin. That is the purpose of h3 in this structure [I].
